title: Java interop, bytecode, K2, compiler plugins
scopeHtml: Scope: how Kotlin looks from Java (Jvm* annotations, checked exceptions, wildcards), reading bytecode, metadata and reflection cost, the K2 compiler and Kotlin 2.x language features, compiler plugins, KAPT vs KSP. Versions verified against kotlinlang.org "What's new" pages for 2.0 through 2.4 (2.4.0 released July 2026).

questions.promptHtml: I have fun formatPrice(...) and val DEFAULT_CURRENCY at the top level of PriceUtils.kt. How does a Java class call them, and how do I control the name Java sees?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know that the JVM has no top-level functions and that Kotlin invents a facade class you may need to name deliberately.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The JVM only has classes, so the compiler puts every top-level declaration of PriceUtils.kt into a synthetic final class PriceUtilsKt as static members. Java calls PriceUtilsKt.formatPrice(...) and PriceUtilsKt.getDEFAULT_CURRENCY(). I rename the facade with @file:JvmName("PriceUtils"), and if several files should share one facade I add @file:JvmMultifileClass with the same name. Private top-level declarations are still emitted but private to that class.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The facade class name is <FileName>Kt. Rename the file and every Java call site breaks, which is a silent binary-compatibility hazard for libraries.
  • Top-level val becomes a private static field plus a public static getter. var adds a static setter. const val becomes a public static final field with no getter, and its value is inlined by javac at call sites.
  • Top-level extension functions become static methods whose first parameter is the receiver: fun String.slugify() is PriceUtilsKt.slugify(String) in Java.
  • @JvmMultifileClass makes the compiler emit one facade that delegates to per-file "part" classes (PriceUtils__PriceUtilsKt). Useful for keeping one Java-facing name while splitting code across files; the stdlib uses it (CollectionsKt).
PriceUtils.kt                         Java sees
------------------------------        -----------------------------------------
fun formatPrice(c: Long): String  ->  public static String formatPrice(long c)
val DEFAULT_CURRENCY = "INR"      ->  private static final String DEFAULT_CURRENCY
                                      public static String getDEFAULT_CURRENCY()
const val MAX_ITEMS = 50          ->  public static final int MAX_ITEMS = 50
fun String.slugify(): String      ->  public static String slugify(String $this$slugify)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@file:JvmName("PriceUtils")
package com.shop.util

const val MAX_ITEMS = 50
val DEFAULT_CURRENCY = "INR"

fun formatPrice(cents: Long): String = "%.2f".format(cents / 100.0)
// Java: PriceUtils.formatPrice(1999L); PriceUtils.getDEFAULT_CURRENCY(); PriceUtils.MAX_ITEMS

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting @file:JvmName after the package line. File annotations must come before package.
  • Two files with the same @JvmName without @JvmMultifileClass: duplicate class error.
  • Renaming a .kt file in a published library and breaking Java consumers' binaries without noticing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can Java call a top-level internal function? → Yes at the bytecode level: internal compiles to public. Internal members of classes additionally get a mangled name (foo$moduleName) to discourage Java use. Treat internal as "not API" either way.
  2. What happens to a top-level private fun? → Private static method of the facade; if a lambda in another class of the same file calls it, the compiler may generate a synthetic accessor.
  3. How does R8 treat facade classes? → They are ordinary classes; R8 inlines and merges static methods freely, so the facade often disappears in release builds. Only reflection or JNI by name is affected.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "use FileNameKt". The senior adds @JvmMultifileClass, the const vs getter difference, that file names are part of a library's binary API, and that tools like the binary-compatibility-validator catch facade renames.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shared Kotlin module renamed Extensions.kt to StringExt.kt; a Java feature module compiled against the old artifact crashed with NoClassDefFoundError: ExtensionsKt on a stale build cache path until clean rebuild.

questions.promptHtml: Why does Java have to write Analytics.Companion.track(...) or Logger.INSTANCE.log(...), and what does @JvmStatic actually change in the bytecode?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates "I add @JvmStatic because Java complained" from understanding that Kotlin objects are real instances.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An object is a class with a static INSTANCE field, and a companion object is a nested class Companion with a static Companion field on the outer class. Their members are instance methods, so Java must go through INSTANCE or Companion. @JvmStatic makes the compiler also emit a real static method: on the outer class for a companion, on the object class itself for an object. The instance method stays, and the static one delegates to it (or the reverse for objects). Kotlin callers do not change at all.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• object Logger { fun log() } compiles to public final class Logger { public static final Logger INSTANCE; private Logger(); public final void log(); static { INSTANCE = new Logger(); } }. Initialization happens in <clinit>, so it is lazy (first access to the class) and thread-safe via JVM class-init locking.
  • Companion: class Analytics { companion object { fun track() } } gives Analytics.Companion (nested class) and public static final Analytics.Companion Companion on Analytics.
  • With @JvmStatic fun track() inside the companion, the compiler adds public static void track() on Analytics that calls Companion.track(). Both exist; that is one extra method per annotated member (method count matters slightly on huge apps, mostly irrelevant after R8).
  • @JvmStatic on a companion property generates static getter/setter on the outer class. For a field without accessors use @JvmField or const.
  • Named companion (companion object Factory) changes the Java name to Analytics.Factory.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Analytics private constructor() {
    companion object {
        @JvmStatic fun track(event: String) { /* ... */ }   // Java: Analytics.track("x")
        fun flush() { /* ... */ }                            // Java: Analytics.Companion.flush()
    }
}

object Clock {
    @JvmStatic fun nowMs(): Long = System.currentTimeMillis()  // Java: Clock.nowMs()
    fun uptime(): Long = 0L                                     // Java: Clock.INSTANCE.uptime()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing @JvmStatic makes the Kotlin member static. The companion instance still exists and holds state.
  • Annotating members of a regular class with @JvmStatic: compile error, only allowed in objects/companions.
  • Interface companions: @JvmStatic there needs JVM target 1.8+ and produces a static interface method, which older tools/desugaring may handle differently.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is object initialization thread-safe? → Yes, JVM class initialization is synchronized; but anything the init block touches (e.g. Android Context) is your problem.
  2. Why would a framework need @JvmStatic? → Frameworks that look for static methods by reflection or annotation (JUnit @BeforeClass/@JvmStatic in companion, @BindingAdapter in data binding, @Provides in Dagger object modules historically) require a true static.
  3. Does @JvmStatic cost anything at runtime? → One extra delegating method; R8 typically inlines it. The real cost of companions is the extra class and its init, not the annotation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "@JvmStatic makes it static for Java." The senior explains INSTANCE/Companion fields, that both methods exist, why frameworks with static lookup need it, and class-init laziness/thread safety.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A JUnit4 @ClassRule declared in a companion without @JvmField/@JvmStatic was silently ignored because JUnit requires a public static field, so a Testcontainers-style rule never started and tests failed with connection errors that looked like infra flakiness.

questions.promptHtml: From Java, what is the difference between a Kotlin val, a const val, a @JvmField val, and a lateinit var?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know Kotlin properties are accessor pairs and when a raw field is exposed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A normal Kotlin property is a private field plus getX()/setX(), so Java calls the getter. const val is only for primitives and String known at compile time; it becomes a public static final field and Java inlines the value. @JvmField removes the accessors and makes the field itself public, which is what frameworks like JUnit rules or some serializers need. lateinit var already exposes its field publicly with the setter's visibility, plus a getter that throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException if unset.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Kotlin Java view Notes
val name: String (class) private final String name; public String getName() getter may be custom
var count = 0 private field + getCount()/setCount(int)
val isReady: Boolean isReady() is prefix kept, setter would be setReady
const val TAG = "x" (top-level/object) public static final String TAG = "x" value inlined into Java and Kotlin callers
@JvmField val id: Int public final int id no getter; cannot be private, open, override, have custom accessor, or be const/lateinit
lateinit var repo: Repo public field repo + getRepo() (throws if null) + setRepo() field visibility follows setter
  • @JvmField in a companion object puts a static field on the outer class (Analytics.CONFIG), not on Companion.
  • @JvmRecord (JVM target 16+) is the other direction of "raw Java shape": a @JvmRecord data class compiles to a java.lang.Record with record components, so Java sees point.x() accessors. It cannot extend a class and all properties must be val in the primary constructor. On Android, record support depends on your D8/desugaring setup; verify before relying on it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class LoginTest {
    @get:Rule                 // annotate the getter, OR:
    val rule1 = TemporaryFolder()

    @JvmField @Rule           // expose public field (JUnit4 accepts public fields)
    val rule2 = TemporaryFolder()

    @Rule                     // broken: annotation lands on the private field; JUnit says "must be public"
    val rule3 = TemporaryFolder()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• @Rule val rule = ... without @get: or @JvmField: JUnit error "The @Rule 'rule' must be public".
  • Expecting const val changes in a library to reach consumers without recompiling them (inlined values; detail belongs to the properties chunk).
  • Using @JvmField everywhere "for performance": ART and R8 already inline trivial getters.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't @JvmField be on an open property? → A field cannot be overridden; open properties need virtual getters.
  2. How do you annotate the setter parameter or backing field specifically? → Use-site targets: @field:, @get:, @set:, @param:, @setparam:, and since Kotlin 2.2 the @all: meta-target (preview in 2.2, stable in 2.4).
  3. Does a value class property exposed to Java work? → Getter name is mangled and it returns the underlying type; see the value-class chunk. Kotlin 2.2 added experimental @JvmExposeBoxed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer knows @JvmField "removes the getter". The senior lists restrictions, the use-site target story, companion static placement, and knows inlining makes the perf argument mostly moot.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams lose hours to Room/JUnit/Espresso annotations landing on the wrong JVM element; checking the decompiled class (see Q218) shows exactly where the annotation went.

questions.promptHtml: What does @JvmOverloads generate, what are its limits, and when should a library not use it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Default arguments are a Kotlin-only concept; this checks if you know how they are compiled and the binary-compatibility consequences.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin compiles a function with defaults into the full-parameter method plus a synthetic foo$default(..., int mask, Object marker) that fills in defaults based on a bitmask. Java can't call the synthetic one, so it must pass everything. @JvmOverloads generates additional overloads by dropping defaulted parameters from the end, one at a time. It does not generate every combination, only trailing prefixes. For libraries it locks in parameter order, and adding a new default parameter later changes the overload set, so I decide deliberately.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• For fun show(msg: String, duration: Int = 2000, gravity: Int = 0) the compiler emits:
    • show(String, int, int) (the real one)
    • show$default(String, int, int, int mask, Object) (synthetic, used by Kotlin callers)
    • with @JvmOverloads: show(String, int) and show(String), each calling the real one with defaults.
  • N defaulted params give N extra overloads. Default expressions are evaluated inside the generated code, so a default that reads mutable state is evaluated at call time, not compile time.
  • Works on constructors (class X @JvmOverloads constructor(...)), which is the classic custom View use, but generated constructors chain to the full one with the Kotlin defaults, not to super(context, attrs). That bites with View theming (see Q228).
  • Not allowed on interface abstract methods or on abstract members.
  • Binary compatibility: adding a param with a default at the end of a Kotlin function changes the JVM signature of the main method. Kotlin source callers recompile fine; already-compiled callers break with NoSuchMethodError. @JvmOverloads happens to keep the old shorter signatures alive, which is sometimes used intentionally. Kotlin 2.4 added experimental @IntroducedAt to generate hidden overloads specifically for this compatibility problem.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Toaster {
    @JvmOverloads
    fun show(msg: String, durationMs: Int = 2000, gravity: Int = 0) { /* ... */ }
}
// Java: toaster.show("hi"); toaster.show("hi", 3500); toaster.show("hi", 3500, Gravity.TOP)
// Java cannot do show("hi", gravity = TOP) - no named args, and no show(String, gravity) overload exists.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting overloads for skipping a middle parameter.
  • Overload ambiguity: two defaults of compatible types can collide with an existing hand-written overload ("conflicting overloads").
  • Using it on View constructors without thinking about defStyleAttr defaults.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the mask in $default? → An int bitmask, one bit per parameter, marking which arguments were omitted; extra ints are added after 32 params.
  2. Why not a builder for Java callers instead? → For many optional params a builder or a config object is clearer and evolves without breaking signatures.
  3. Does @JvmOverloads help Kotlin callers? → No, Kotlin uses $default; it only adds Java-visible overloads.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "makes default params work in Java". The senior describes $default + mask, trailing-only overloads, binary-compatibility effects, and when to prefer a builder.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Kotlin SDK added timeoutMs: Int = 30_000 at the end of fetch(); a prebuilt Java plugin compiled against the old version crashed with NoSuchMethodError because nobody ran an API dump check.

questions.promptHtml: Kotlin has no checked exceptions. What problems does that cause when Java calls Kotlin, and what does @Throws do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real mixed codebases break here: Java can't catch what the signature doesn't declare.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin lets any function throw any exception without declaring it, and the compiled method has no throws clause. Java's compiler then refuses catch (IOException e) around that call, because from its point of view the try block can't throw IOException, so Java devs catch Exception broadly or not at all. @Throws(IOException::class) adds the throws clause to the JVM signature so Java can and must handle it. It matters also for dynamic proxies and for overriding Java interfaces.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Checked exceptions are a javac rule, not a JVM rule. The JVM throws anything anywhere. Kotlin simply skips the check.
  • Java compile error: "exception java.io.IOException is never thrown in body of corresponding try statement".
  • java.lang.reflect.Proxy: if an invocation handler throws a checked exception not declared on the interface method, the proxy wraps it in UndeclaredThrowableException. A Kotlin interface used through a Java proxy therefore changes the exception type callers see (see Q231).
  • Overriding a Java method that declares throws IOException in Kotlin: you can throw freely; Kotlin does not copy the clause unless you add @Throws. Java callers holding the Java interface type are fine because the interface declares it.
  • @Throws is also important on Kotlin/Native for Swift/ObjC interop, and for suspend functions called from Swift; mentioned only for completeness.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FileStore(private val dir: java.io.File) {
    @Throws(java.io.IOException::class)
    fun read(name: String): ByteArray = java.io.File(dir, name).readBytes()
}
try {
    byte[] data = store.read("cfg.json");
} catch (IOException e) {   // compiles only because of @Throws
    showError(e);
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping everything in RuntimeException "for Java" and losing the type.
  • Forgetting @Throws on public API of a library that Java clients consume, then getting complaints that they can't catch IO errors.
  • Believing @Throws forces Kotlin callers to handle it. It does not.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is it a good idea to use Java's sneaky throw from Kotlin? → It's what Kotlin does by default; the problem is only communication with Java callers.
  2. How should a Kotlin library signal recoverable errors instead? → Sealed result types or documented exceptions; for Java-heavy consumers, @Throws on the public surface.
  3. Does runCatching interact with this? → No interop change; it catches Throwable, including cancellation; that's the cancellation chunk's topic.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "add @Throws for Java". The senior explains it's a javac rule, the "never thrown" compile error, proxy UndeclaredThrowableException, and API design choices.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Java code catching Exception around a Kotlin call also swallowed a NullPointerException from a bug, turning a crash into a silent empty screen for weeks.

questions.promptHtml: Why does this fail to compile: fun List<String>.joinIds(): String and fun List<Int>.joinIds(): String in the same file, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows understanding of erasure at the JVM signature level and of @JvmName beyond renaming for Java.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both compile to static String joinIds(List) because generics are erased, so the JVM would see two identical methods. Kotlin reports "Platform declaration clash: the following declarations have the same JVM signature". I give one or both a different JVM name with @JvmName("joinStringIds"). Kotlin callers still call joinIds() because Kotlin resolves on the full generic type; only the bytecode name differs. The same tool fixes property getter clashes like a val x with a fun getX().

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Kotlin overload resolution uses generic types at compile time; the JVM method descriptor ((Ljava/util/List;)Ljava/lang/String;) has no type arguments. Two Kotlin functions are legal for Kotlin but illegal for the class file.
  • Typical clashes:
    • Generic-only overloads (above).
    • Property val name vs function fun getName() in the same class.
    • Extension property on a type vs top-level function with the getter's name.
    • Inherited Java getter plus Kotlin property.
  • @JvmName uses: rename top-level facade (@file:JvmName), rename getter/setter (@get:JvmName("isEnabledFlag")), resolve clashes, and replace the mangled JVM name the compiler gives functions that take value-class parameters (foo-<hash>), which makes them callable from Java.
  • Cannot be used on open/override members (would break virtual dispatch naming).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@JvmName("joinStringIds")
fun List<String>.joinIds(): String = joinToString(",")

@JvmName("joinIntIds")
fun List<Int>.joinIds(): String = joinToString(",") { it.toString() }

class Flags {
    @get:JvmName("isDarkMode") val darkMode: Boolean = false   // Java: flags.isDarkMode()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Renaming the Kotlin function instead, which uglifies Kotlin API for a JVM constraint.
  • Putting @JvmName on an override (error).
  • Forgetting that @JvmName on public library API is a binary-compatible name you now must keep.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why doesn't Java have this problem? → It does; Java also rejects such overloads ("name clash: same erasure").
  2. What about fun foo(x: Int) vs fun foo(x: Int?)? → Different descriptors (I vs Ljava/lang/Integer;), so no clash.
  3. How do mangled names for value classes relate? → Kotlin mangles names like foo-abc123 for functions taking value classes to avoid exactly this kind of clash and to stop Java calling them; @JvmName can override that.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer fixes it with @JvmName by trial. The senior explains the descriptor, lists clash types, and treats JVM names as API.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Shared util modules with Flow<A>.asUiState() and Flow<B>.asUiState() regularly hit this; teams adopt a convention of @JvmName("asUiStateA") on all generic-only overloads.

questions.promptHtml: Dagger fails with "cannot be provided without an @Provides-annotated method" for a Map<Class<out ViewModel>, Provider<ViewModel>> that clearly is bound. Why, and what do @JvmSuppressWildcards and @JvmWildcard do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic real-world interop bug; shows you understand how Kotlin declaration-site variance becomes Java wildcards.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin's List<out E> and Map<K, out V> are covariant at the declaration site. When Kotlin emits a Java signature for a parameter of such a type, it adds wildcards so Java callers get the same flexibility: Map<Class<? extends ViewModel>, ? extends Provider<ViewModel>>. Dagger matches types exactly, and the bound type has no wildcard, so the lookup fails. @JvmSuppressWildcards tells the compiler not to emit those wildcards; @JvmWildcard forces them where they would normally be omitted, like return types.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rules the Kotlin compiler uses for JVM signatures:

  • Parameters: wildcard added for a covariant (out) or contravariant (in) type parameter position, unless the type argument is final (e.g. List<String> stays List<String> because String is final, nothing can extend it).
  • Return types: no wildcards (Java callers would have to deal with ? extends on results, which is awkward).
  • Provider<ViewModel> is not final, and it is in Map's out V position, so it gets ? extends.
Kotlin:  fun inject(map: Map<Class<out ViewModel>, Provider<ViewModel>>)
Java  :  void inject(Map<Class<? extends ViewModel>, ? extends Provider<ViewModel>> map)
                       ^ from explicit out          ^ from Map's declaration-site out V
With @JvmSuppressWildcards on the type:
Java  :  void inject(Map<Class<? extends ViewModel>, Provider<ViewModel>> map)
         (use-site `out` written by you stays as a wildcard; only the implicit ones are removed)
  • Annotation can go on a type, parameter, function, or class (applies to everything inside).
  • Same issue appears with Dagger Set<Interceptor> multibindings, Retrofit/Guice generic injections, and any Java framework that reflects on Type.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ViewModelFactory @Inject constructor(
    private val creators: Map<Class<out ViewModel>, @JvmSuppressWildcards Provider<ViewModel>>
) : ViewModelProvider.Factory {
    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
    override fun <T : ViewModel> create(modelClass: Class<T>): T =
        creators.getValue(modelClass).get() as T
}

@Module
interface NetModule {
    @Multibinds fun interceptors(): Set<@JvmSuppressWildcards okhttp3.Interceptor>
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Annotating the outer Map and expecting the explicit out in Class<out ViewModel> to vanish too. It is a use-site projection you wrote, which is kept.
  • Thinking this is Dagger-specific. Any Type-based matching (Guice, Gson TypeToken lookups) can hit it.
  • Sprinkling it on the whole class without understanding, then a Java caller can no longer pass List<SubType>.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Kotlin add wildcards at all? → So Java callers get the covariance Kotlin users have; otherwise List<Dog> couldn't be passed where List<Animal> is declared.
  2. Why does List<String> not get one? → String is final; ? extends String adds nothing.
  3. Does Hilt still need this? → Hilt's generated code covers the standard ViewModel map, but your own multibindings in Kotlin still do.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer copies @JvmSuppressWildcards from Stack Overflow. The senior explains declaration-site variance, the final-type and return-type exceptions, and why exact type matching fails.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Kotlin migration of a Dagger module turned a working Java Set<Interceptor> multibinding into a compile failure in a 300-module build; the fix was one annotation, the diagnosis took a day without knowing this rule.

questions.promptHtml: How do you find out what a piece of Kotlin actually compiles to, and what do you look for when you read it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers settle "is this expensive?" and "where did my annotation go?" by reading bytecode, not by guessing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In Android Studio I use Tools > Kotlin > Show Kotlin Bytecode, then Decompile to get Java-like source. For exact detail I run javap -c -p on the class in build/tmp/kotlin-classes, and for release behavior I look at the dexed, R8-processed output with the APK Analyzer or r8's mapping. I look for hidden allocations (boxing, lambda objects, iterators), synthetic methods ($default, accessors), null-check intrinsics, where annotations landed, and generated classes from plugins.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Workflow by question:

Question Tool
What does the compiler generate for this function? Show Kotlin Bytecode (IDE), Decompile
Exact instructions, descriptors, flags (synthetic, bridge) javap -c -p -v Foo.class
What survives into the APK, after R8 inlining/merging APK Analyzer (dex view, "Show bytecode"), retrace with mapping.txt
Is it allocating at runtime? Android Studio Memory Profiler allocation tracking, Perfetto heap profile

Things worth recognizing in decompiled output:

  • Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter(x, "x") at public entry points (null-safety; owned by the type-system chunk).
  • Integer.valueOf(...) / Boxing.boxInt(...): boxing, e.g. a nullable Int? or generic T holding an Int.
  • new Function1<...> or invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory: lambda representation (Kotlin 2.0 switched default to invokedynamic; lambda chunk owns the details).
  • Ref.IntRef: captured var.
  • access$getFoo synthetic accessors: private members touched from a lambda/nested class.
  • $default methods and bitmask: default arguments.
  • @Metadata(mv=..., k=..., d1=..., d2=...) on every class: Kotlin's own type info (Q219).
  • Suspend functions: extra Continuation parameter and a state machine (coroutine chunks own this).

Decompiled Java is a reconstruction; it can show code that doesn't compile (labels, $this$apply names, Unit.INSTANCE expressions). Trust javap when the decompiler output looks impossible.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Question: does this allocate per call?
fun sumPositive(xs: List<Int>): Int = xs.filter { it > 0 }.sumOf { it }
// Bytecode shows: new ArrayList (filter), Iterator objects, Integer.intValue() unboxing per element.
// IntArray + a manual loop has none of those; whether it matters depends on list size and call frequency.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading debug bytecode and concluding about release performance. R8 inlines, removes, and merges a lot.
  • Trusting the decompiler's Java literally; it is a best-effort rendering.
  • Micro-optimizing from bytecode without a profiler trace showing the code is hot.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where are the compiled Kotlin classes in a Gradle Android build? → Under build/tmp/kotlin-classes/<variant> (Java classes go to build/intermediates/javac/...).
  2. How do you inspect what R8 did to a method? → Build release, open the APK in APK Analyzer, look at the dex, and use mapping.txt or the R8 -printconfiguration/-whyareyoukeeping rules.
  3. How do you prove an allocation matters? → Allocation tracking in the profiler during the scenario, or a Macrobenchmark/Microbenchmark with allocation counts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer knows the "Show Kotlin Bytecode" menu. The senior has a tool per question, knows what common patterns look like, and checks release (R8) output plus a profiler before claiming cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team argued for weeks about inline vs not on a hot list-binding helper; a 10-minute look at dex output plus a Microbenchmark settled that R8 already inlined it.

questions.promptHtml: What is the @kotlin.Metadata annotation, why does it matter for reflection and R8, and what does using kotlin-reflect cost on Android?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Connects compiler output, release shrinking, and app startup. Many mysterious release-only crashes live here.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The JVM class format can't express Kotlin-only facts: nullability, val vs var, default arguments, data/sealed/value classes, extension receivers, suspend, internal. Kotlin stores these in a @Metadata annotation with protobuf-encoded strings on every class. kotlin-reflect (full KClass reflection like memberProperties, primaryConstructor, isData) parses that metadata at runtime. On Android that means a large library, slow first calls (class loading plus parsing), and dependence on R8 keeping both the metadata and the names. Foo::class.java and Foo::class.simpleName-style light reflection don't need kotlin-reflect.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Metadata fields: k (kind: class, file facade, synthetic class, multifile part), mv (metadata version), d1 (protobuf payload), d2 (string table), xi (flags).
  • Consumers: kotlin-reflect, the Kotlin compiler itself when you depend on a compiled jar (so libraries must keep it), kotlinx-metadata-jvm / kotlin-metadata-jvm tools, Moshi's reflective KotlinJsonAdapterFactory, Jackson Kotlin module, some DI frameworks.
  • R8: by default metadata of shrunk/obfuscated classes may be removed or no longer match renamed members. You keep it with -keep class kotlin.Metadata { *; } plus keeping the classes you reflect on (-keep/-keepclassmembers). R8 can rewrite metadata for kept classes. Kotlin 2.4 enables "annotations in metadata" by default on JVM; not relevant to most app code.
  • Cost profile of kotlin-reflect:
    • Size: the jar is a few MB uncompressed before shrinking (around 3 MB in recent versions); R8 removes much of it, but full reflection keeps a non-trivial chunk.
    • Time: first KClass.memberProperties on a class loads reflection infrastructure and parses the protobuf; on a mid-range device this is tens of milliseconds for the first few classes, hundreds if it happens for many models during startup. Subsequent calls hit caches.
    • Measure it, don't trust these ranges: startup Macrobenchmark plus a Perfetto trace with Trace.beginSection around the deserialization.
  • Alternatives that avoid runtime reflection: kotlinx.serialization (compiler plugin), Moshi codegen (KSP), Room/Hilt (KSP-generated code).
Light reflection (no kotlin-reflect):     Full reflection (needs kotlin-reflect):
  Foo::class.java                           Foo::class.memberProperties
  Foo::class.java.getDeclaredFields()      Foo::class.primaryConstructor
  Foo::class.simpleName (JVM)              KProperty.returnType.isMarkedNullable
  obj::class.qualifiedName (JVM)           KParameter.isOptional (default args)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Needs kotlin-reflect and metadata kept:
val fields = User::class.memberProperties.map { it.name }

// Cheap, Java reflection only:
val javaFields = User::class.java.declaredFields.map { it.name }
// Better: no reflection at all - generated serializer
@kotlinx.serialization.Serializable data class User(val id: Long, val name: String = "")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding kotlin-reflect "because Moshi asked for it" without considering codegen.
  • Keeping metadata but obfuscating member names, so kotlin-reflect sees names that don't match.
  • Running full reflection in Application.onCreate for config parsing, then wondering why cold start regressed.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do libraries need metadata even without reflection? → The Kotlin compiler of the consumer reads it to see nullability, defaults, inline bodies, etc.; strip it from a published AAR and Kotlin consumers see Java-like platform types.
  2. What does KotlinReflectionNotSupportedError mean? → You called a full-reflection API without kotlin-reflect on the classpath.
  3. How would you detect hidden kotlin-reflect use? → Check the dependency graph (./gradlew :app:dependencies), search dex for kotlin.reflect.jvm.internal, and trace startup.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "reflection is slow". The senior explains what metadata contains and who reads it, the R8 keep story, light vs full reflection, and replaces runtime reflection with compile-time generation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A release-only crash where Moshi's reflective adapter produced nulls for non-null fields came from R8 renaming properties while metadata was kept for the original names; switching to codegen removed both the crash and kotlin-reflect.

questions.promptHtml: What is K2, what changed with Kotlin 2.0, and where are we now?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic awareness of the toolchain you ship with; whether you track the ecosystem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: K2 is the rewritten Kotlin compiler frontend, the part that parses, resolves names and types, and reports errors. Its internal representation is called FIR (Frontend Intermediate Representation). It became the default and stable in Kotlin 2.0.0 (May 2024). One frontend now serves JVM, Native, JS and Wasm, feeding the existing IR backends. It's faster at analysis, has more consistent rules (notably better smart casts), and is the base for new language features. K1 was kept as an opt-out via language version 1.9 for a while; Kotlin 2.4 (July 2026) removed language version 1.9, so K1 is gone.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
K1 era (<= 1.9)                         K2 era (>= 2.0)
source -> PSI -> K1 frontend (BindingContext)  source -> PSI -> FIR (K2 frontend)
        -> psi2ir -> IR -> JVM/JS/Native        -> fir2ir -> IR -> JVM/JS/Native/Wasm backends
  • The JVM IR backend had already become default in Kotlin 1.5; 2.0 replaced the frontend.
  • FIR is a tree with resolved types attached through phases (raw FIR, imports, supertypes, types, bodies, checkers). K1 used a big map ("BindingContext") from PSI to semantic info, which was slow and hard to keep consistent.
  • User-visible consequences:
    • Compile speed: JetBrains reported large frontend speedups (headline numbers up to roughly 2x on some projects); real Android builds see less because KAPT, dexing, and resource processing don't change.
    • Smart-cast and resolution improvements (Q221), some new errors where K1 was unsound.
    • Compiler plugins had to move to the K2 plugin API (FIR extensions); that's why Compose compiler, kapt and KSP had their own migrations.
    • IDE: K2 mode in IntelliJ/Android Studio uses the same frontend for analysis.
  • Version timeline (verify against kotlinlang.org "What's new" when quoting): 2.0 (May 2024) K2 stable; 2.1 (Nov 2024) language previews; 2.2 (Jun 2025) several of those stable; 2.3 (Dec 2025); 2.4 (Jul 2026).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// gradle.properties / build: nothing to enable on 2.x - K2 is default.
// On 2.0-2.3 you could fall back with:
kotlin { compilerOptions { languageVersion.set(org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle.dsl.KotlinVersion.KOTLIN_1_9) } }
// Not available from 2.4: language version 1.9 is no longer supported.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking K2 changes runtime performance of the app. It mostly changes compile time and diagnostics; bytecode differences are minor (some codegen defaults changed separately, e.g. lambdas via invokedynamic).
  • Confusing "K2" with "Kotlin 2.0 language features". Most new syntax came later (2.1+).
  • Assuming every compiler plugin upgraded for free.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's the difference between frontend and backend? → Frontend: syntax, resolution, type inference, diagnostics. Backend: lowering IR to bytecode/JS/native.
  2. Does K2 change the stdlib or binary format? → No new runtime requirement; metadata version bumped, older compilers may not read 2.x metadata (forward compatibility is limited to one version).
  3. Why did KSP need KSP2? → KSP1 was built on K1 internals; KSP2 uses the Analysis API on K2. KSP1 is deprecated and doesn't support Kotlin 2.3+.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "new faster compiler". The senior can draw the pipeline, explain FIR vs BindingContext, separate compile-time from runtime effects, and knows the plugin ecosystem consequences and timeline.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams upgrading to 2.0 found their bottleneck was KAPT running stub generation through K1 fallback, so K2's speedup barely showed until KAPT was removed (see Q233).

questions.promptHtml: Give concrete examples of code that K2 smart-casts but K1 didn't.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical K2 knowledge beyond the headline; shows you have actually migrated code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin 2.0 smart-casts in more places: when the type check is stored in a local val and used later; after || between type checks, it casts to the closest common supertype; inside lambdas of inline functions, because the compiler assumes they run in place; for function-type properties when calling them; after try/catch/finally with better flow tracking; and with increment/decrement on vars. Smart-cast stability rules themselves (no casts on open or custom-getter properties, mutable vars captured by concurrently running lambdas) didn't change.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Case K1 K2 (2.0+)
val isCat = animal is Cat; if (isCat) animal.purr() error, needs cast smart cast
if (s is Postponed || s is Declined) s.signal() (both implement Status) cast to Any cast to common supertype Status
var x: Any? modified inside run { } then checked conservatively unstable inline lambda treated as called in place, flow tracked
val provider: (() -> Unit)? then if (provider != null) provider() worked only for some forms consistent
catch block after a var was reassigned in try sometimes unsound tracks possible reassignment correctly
  • Stability rules (unchanged, covered in the type-system chunk): only stable values are smart-cast: local vals, val properties with default getters in the same module that are not open, local vars not captured in a lambda that modifies them.
  • Data-flow-based exhaustiveness checks for when became Stable in Kotlin 2.3: if earlier code already excluded a sealed subtype (e.g. early return), when no longer needs that branch.
  • Some K1-accepted code is now an error because K1 was unsound (e.g. smart cast after a var was reassigned in a try that might throw). That shows up during migration.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface Status { fun signal() }
class Postponed : Status { override fun signal() {} }
class Declined : Status { override fun signal() {} }

fun handle(animal: Any, s: Any) {
    val isString = animal is String
    if (isString) println(animal.length)         // K2: OK, K1: error

    if (s is Postponed || s is Declined) s.signal() // K2: s is Status
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting smart casts across module boundaries or on open properties now; still not allowed.
  • Assuming non-inline lambdas get the "called in place" treatment; only inline functions (or contracts) do.
  • Writing new code that only compiles on K2 in a library that consumers might build from source with older compilers (rare on Android, common in KMP libs).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't K2 smart-cast a var captured by a non-inline lambda? → The lambda could run later or on another thread and change it; the check is not stable.
  2. How does a contract relate? → callsInPlace lets a non-stdlib inline-like function promise how a lambda runs; see the contracts chunk.
  3. Did K2 break anything around smart casts? → Yes, it reports errors where K1 incorrectly allowed casts; those are real latent bugs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer knows "smart casts got better". The senior gives three concrete cases, knows stability rules didn't change, and mentions new errors and 2.3 data-flow exhaustiveness.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: During migration, a few modules failed with new smart-cast errors in try/catch blocks; each was a genuine case where a variable could be stale after an exception.

questions.promptHtml: Which language features arrived after Kotlin 2.0, what do they do, and which are stable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks if you track the language and know the difference between Stable, Beta, Preview and Experimental before using a feature in production.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Three previews landed in 2.1 and became Stable in 2.2: guard conditions in when (is X if cond ->), non-local break/continue inside inline lambdas, and multi-dollar string interpolation for text full of $. Context parameters were a preview in 2.2 and are Stable in 2.4 except explicit context arguments and callable references. Kotlin 2.3 added experimental explicit backing fields and an experimental unused-return-value checker; explicit backing fields are Stable in 2.4. Nested type aliases were Beta in 2.2 and Stable in 2.3. In production I use Stable features freely and treat Preview/Experimental as opt-in behind a compiler flag, with no use in published library APIs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Feature 2.1 2.2 2.3 2.4
Guard conditions in when Preview (-Xwhen-guards) Stable Stable Stable
Non-local break/continue Preview Stable Stable Stable
Multi-dollar interpolation Preview Stable Stable Stable
Context parameters - Preview (-Xcontext-parameters) Preview Stable (explicit context args & callable refs excluded)
Nested type aliases - Beta Stable Stable
Data-flow exhaustiveness for when - - Stable Stable
Explicit backing fields - - Experimental Stable
Unused return value checker - - Experimental (-Xreturn-value-checker) Experimental
Collection literals [a, b] - - - Experimental (-Xcollection-literals)

Note: the flag names for 2.1 previews are from memory of the 2.1 notes; check whatsnew21 before quoting them.

What each does:

  • Guard conditions: add a boolean condition to a when branch with a subject, keeping exhaustiveness checks on the sealed type.
  • Non-local break/continue: break/continue inside a lambda passed to an inline function (e.g. forEach, let) now affects the enclosing loop.
  • Multi-dollar interpolation: $$"..." means you need $$name to interpolate, so single $ is literal. Great for JSON Schema, GraphQL, shell snippets.
  • Explicit backing fields: val state: StateFlow<T> with field = MutableStateFlow(...), replacing the _state/state pair; inside the class, state smart-casts to the mutable type.
  • Unused return value checker: warns when a non-Unit result is ignored (e.g. calling list.plus(x) and discarding it, or copy() without using it).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface UiEvent { data class Click(val id: Int, val long: Boolean) : UiEvent; data object Back : UiEvent }

fun route(e: UiEvent) = when (e) {
    is UiEvent.Click if e.long -> "context menu ${e.id}"   // guard condition
    is UiEvent.Click -> "open ${e.id}"
    UiEvent.Back -> "back"
}

fun firstValid(rows: List<String?>) {
    for (r in rows) {
        r?.let { if (it.isBlank()) continue }               // non-local continue (2.2+)
        println(r)
    }
}

val schema = $$"""{ "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema", "title": "$${"User"}" }"""

class SearchViewModel {
    val query: kotlinx.coroutines.flow.StateFlow<String>
        field = kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow("")  // explicit backing field (2.4 Stable)
    fun onQuery(q: String) { query.value = q }               // smart-cast to MutableStateFlow inside class
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a Preview feature in a shared module while other modules or consumers compile with a different flag set.
  • Assuming guard conditions work on when without a subject. They are for subject when; without a subject you already have arbitrary conditions.
  • Mixing up multi-dollar count: with $$"..." you need exactly two $ to interpolate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do Experimental/Preview/Beta/Stable mean? → Experimental: may change or be dropped, opt-in only. Preview (Alpha in older docs): design mostly settled, still opt-in. Beta: close to stable, migration help promised. Stable: compatibility guaranteed under Kotlin's evolution rules.
  2. Why use the return value checker? → Catches discarded results of pure functions like immutable collection ops or copy(); val _ = f() silences intentionally.
  3. Do explicit backing fields replace asStateFlow()? → They remove the second property; Java/other modules still only see the declared StateFlow type. A caller could still downcast, same as before.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer remembers one feature. The senior can state per-version status, explains the stability levels, and has a policy for adopting non-stable features.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One team enabled -Xcontext-parameters in 2.2 in one module; the IDE and a static analysis tool lagged, CI lint crashed on the syntax, and the feature was backed out until tooling caught up.

questions.promptHtml: What are context parameters, how are they different from context receivers and extension receivers, and would you use them in an Android codebase?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Newest major language feature; a senior should reason about API design and adoption risk, not just syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A context parameter is a named or anonymous parameter declared with context(logger: Logger) that callers don't pass explicitly; the compiler resolves it from contexts available at the call site, like an enclosing with(logger) { } or the caller's own context parameters. They replace the earlier experimental context receivers, which put the context into this scope and caused ambiguity. Context parameters are named, so they're explicit at the use site, and anonymous ones _ just forward. Preview in 2.2, Stable in 2.4 except explicit context arguments and callable references. I'd use them for cross-cutting capabilities (logging, transaction scope, a DSL scope), not to hide ordinary dependencies that DI should inject.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Declaration: context(tx: Transaction) fun insert(user: User) { tx.exec(...) }.
  • Call: needs a Transaction in context: with(tx) { insert(u) } or inside another function that declares context(tx: Transaction).
  • Versus extension receiver: an extension has exactly one receiver and it becomes this, so members resolve implicitly. Context parameters don't become this (when named), so you call tx.exec(); that avoids accidental member resolution.
  • Versus context receivers (old, -Xcontext-receivers): those added receivers to this scope; mixing several led to unreadable resolution. Using both flags together is an error; IDE offers migration.
  • Compilation on JVM: context parameters become ordinary leading parameters in the JVM method. From Java you pass them explicitly.
  • 2.4 adds experimental explicit context arguments (sendNotification(emailSender = x)) to resolve ambiguity between overloads.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface Logger { fun log(msg: String) }

context(logger: Logger)
fun syncUser(id: Long) {
    logger.log("sync $id")
    // ...
}

context(_: Logger)          // anonymous: only forwards the context
fun syncAll(ids: List<Long>) = ids.forEach { syncUser(it) }

fun main(logger: Logger) {
    with(logger) { syncAll(listOf(1, 2, 3)) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using context parameters as service locator replacement: dependencies become invisible at call sites and hard to fake in tests.
  • Adopting them in public library API while still Preview (2.2/2.3), forcing consumers onto a flag.
  • Forgetting Java callers see them as plain parameters, in declaration order before the regular ones.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a property have a context parameter? → Yes, properties can declare context(...) but they cannot have a backing field or initializer; they're computed.
  2. What problem does this solve in Compose or coroutines-style APIs? → Scoped capabilities like "only callable inside a transaction" or DSL scopes, enforced by the compiler instead of runtime checks.
  3. How would you roll it out? → Stable version only, team guideline (which interfaces may be context types), lint/detekt support check, start in internal modules.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer shows syntax. The senior explains resolution, the receiver ambiguity it fixes, JVM shape, version status, and an adoption policy tied to DI and testability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Database layers are the strongest use: a context(_: TransactionScope) on DAO helpers makes "called outside a transaction" a compile error instead of a production data-consistency bug.

questions.promptHtml: What is a Kotlin compiler plugin, how is it different from an annotation processor, and what do Compose, kotlinx.serialization, Parcelize and all-open/no-arg do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most of an Android app's "magic" is compiler plugins; seniors should know what runs where and why versions must match.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A compiler plugin runs inside kotlinc and can change the program: add members, rewrite IR, add checks. An annotation processor (KAPT/KSP) can only read declarations and generate new source files; it can't modify existing classes. Compose's plugin rewrites @Composable functions to add a Composer parameter and change groups, skipping and remembering; since Kotlin 2.0 it lives in the Kotlin repo and ships with the same version as Kotlin. kotlinx.serialization generates serializer() and $serializer classes. Parcelize generates writeToParcel/CREATOR. all-open and no-arg make classes open or add a no-arg constructor for frameworks like Spring or JPA.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Plugin Gradle id What it generates/changes Typical pitfall
Compose compiler org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose (Kotlin 2.0+) Adds $composer, $changed params, groups, stability inference, lambda memoization Before 2.0 its version had to match Kotlin exactly via kotlinCompilerExtensionVersion
kotlinx.serialization org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.serialization Companion serializer(), nested $serializer, synthetic constructor honoring defaults Plugin version = Kotlin version; runtime lib versioned separately
Parcelize org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.parcelize (kotlin-parcelize) writeToParcel, describeContents, CREATOR for primary-constructor props Body properties are not parcelled
all-open / kotlin-spring org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.allopen Removes final from annotated classes Mostly backend, not Android
no-arg / kotlin-jpa org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.noarg Synthetic no-arg constructor (callable via reflection only) init blocks aren't run unless invokeInitializers
Power-assert (2.0+, experimental) org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.power-assert Rich assertion messages Test-only
  • Compiler plugins operate on the K2 frontend (FIR extensions for declarations/checkers) and the IR backend (transformations). Versions are tied to the compiler, which is why Kotlin upgrades used to block on Compose compiler releases. Since 2.0, Compose compiler is released with Kotlin, so that coupling is gone.
  • Compose compiler options moved into a composeCompiler { } Gradle block (stability configuration file, reports/metrics). Strong skipping became default in Compose compiler 2.0.20; 2.4 deprecated the StrongSkipping and IntrinsicRemember feature flags at ERROR level.
  • Annotation processors run before/alongside compilation and generate new source; they can't touch existing bodies. KAPT emulates javac processing via Java stubs; KSP reads Kotlin symbols directly (Q226).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// libs.versions.toml-free example, module build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("com.android.application")
    id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose") version "2.2.21"       // same as Kotlin version
    id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.serialization") version "2.2.21"
    id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.parcelize") version "2.2.21"
}
// Version numbers are illustrative; they must equal your Kotlin Gradle plugin version.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Upgrading Kotlin but pinning a plugin to an older version via a separate catalog entry.
  • Thinking kotlinx-serialization-json version must equal Kotlin version. Only the plugin must; the runtime has its own compatibility table.
  • Expecting no-arg constructors to be callable from Kotlin/Java source; they're synthetic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why did Compose need a compiler plugin instead of an annotation processor? → It has to rewrite function signatures and bodies; processors can't modify code.
  2. What happens if a compiler plugin isn't K2-compatible? → The build fails or falls back; that was a main migration blocker in 2024.
  3. With AGP 9, do I still apply kotlin-android? → AGP 9 has built-in Kotlin support; Kotlin 2.3 notes say applying kotlin-android with AGP 9+ is a configuration error. Compiler plugins like Compose are still applied.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists plugins. The senior explains plugin vs processor capability, compiler-version coupling and how 2.0 removed it for Compose, and the concrete pitfall of each.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Before Kotlin 2.0, teams routinely waited weeks after a Kotlin release for a matching Compose compiler; moving it into the Kotlin repo turned that into a single version bump.

questions.promptHtml: Why does kotlinx.serialization respect Kotlin default values and non-null types when Gson doesn't, and what does the compiler plugin actually generate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Ties together compiler plugins, constructors, nullability and R8; Gson-null-in-non-null-field bugs are common (the field-level symptom is covered in the lateinit/casts chunk).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Gson creates objects with Unsafe.allocateInstance when there is no no-arg constructor, then writes fields reflectively. No Kotlin constructor runs, so defaults and null checks are skipped. kotlinx.serialization's compiler plugin generates, at compile time, a $serializer object with a descriptor and serialize/deserialize methods, plus a synthetic constructor that takes a bitmask of which fields were present. Missing fields get their Kotlin default; missing fields without a default throw MissingFieldException; JSON null for a non-null type throws instead of sneaking in. No runtime reflection, so R8 needs very few rules.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
@Serializable data class User(val id: Long, val name: String = "Guest")

Generated (conceptually):
  class User {
    companion object { fun serializer(): KSerializer<User> = `$serializer` }
    object `$serializer` : GeneratedSerializer<User> {
      descriptor = "User" { id: Long (required), name: String (optional) }
      deserialize(decoder): reads elements in a loop, sets bit i in `seen` mask,
                            then calls User(seen, id, name, null)
    }
    // synthetic ctor: if (seen and 0b10 == 0) name = "Guest"
    //                 if (seen and 0b01 == 0) throw MissingFieldException("id")
  }
  • Format-agnostic: the same serializer works with JSON, ProtoBuf, CBOR, Properties; formats are separate libraries.
  • Defaults are not encoded by default (encodeDefaults = false in Json { }), so a field equal to its default is omitted when sending. This matters for backends that require the field (see Q235).
  • Unknown keys throw by default; ignoreUnknownKeys = true is the usual client setting. explicitNulls, coerceInputValues (null or unknown enum value → default) are other common knobs.
  • Polymorphism: sealed classes get automatic polymorphic serializers with a class discriminator ("type"); open polymorphism needs a SerializersModule.
  • R8: the library ships consumer rules; you mainly need to keep things if you look serializers up reflectively via serializer<T>() on generic types or use @Serializable on classes R8 would otherwise strip. Check the library's README for current rules.

Comparison:

Gson Moshi reflect Moshi codegen (KSP) kotlinx.serialization
Runs Kotlin ctor / defaults No Yes (via kotlin-reflect) Yes Yes
Enforces non-null No Yes Yes Yes
Runtime reflection Yes Yes No No
Needs kotlin-reflect No Yes No No
Multiplatform No No No Yes

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@kotlinx.serialization.Serializable
data class Profile(val id: Long, val name: String = "Guest", val tags: List<String> = emptyList())

val json = kotlinx.serialization.json.Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }
val p = json.decodeFromString<Profile>("""{"id": 7}""")   // Profile(7, "Guest", [])
// Gson with the same JSON: name == null (despite String type), tags == null -> NPE later

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding the runtime dependency but not the compiler plugin: Serializer for class 'X' is not found at runtime.
  • Making a property @Transient without a default value: compile error, transient properties need defaults.
  • Assuming encodeDefaults = false is harmless; servers that treat missing as null will see different data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you serialize a third-party class you can't annotate? → Write a custom KSerializer, or a surrogate @Serializable class with @Serializable(with = ...) / contextual serializers.
  2. What does @SerialName change? → The key in the output and descriptor; keeps Kotlin names free and survives R8 renaming (which doesn't matter here since no reflection is used).
  3. Why is it multiplatform-safe? → Everything is generated code over common interfaces; no JVM reflection.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "kotlinx.serialization is Kotlin-friendly". The senior explains Unsafe allocation in Gson, the generated mask-based constructor, default encoding behavior, and the reflection/R8/startup consequences.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Migrating a 400-model app off Gson surfaced dozens of MissingFieldExceptions in QA, each a field the backend sometimes omitted that Gson had been silently nulling into non-null types.

questions.promptHtml: Briefly, how do KAPT and KSP differ, and what should a team on Kotlin 2.x do about KAPT?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Build time is a senior concern; KAPT is the biggest Kotlin-specific build cost in many Android apps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: KAPT runs Java annotation processors on Kotlin code by first generating Java stub files for every Kotlin class, then running javac's processing, which is slow and loses Kotlin-only information. KSP is a Kotlin-native API: processors read Kotlin symbols directly, no stubs, typically around twice as fast for the processing step, and it understands nullability, default args and so on. KAPT is in maintenance mode; its K2 implementation became default in Kotlin 2.1.20 (kapt.use.k2=false to temporarily revert). Room, Hilt/Dagger, Moshi and Glide support KSP. A 2.x team should move every processor to KSP and remove the kapt plugin from each module once its last processor is gone.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
KAPT:  .kt -> [kapt stub gen: Kotlin -> Java stubs] -> javac APT (processors) -> generated .java/.kt -> kotlinc + javac
KSP:   .kt -> [KSP: Kotlin symbol model]  -> processors -> generated .kt/.java -> kotlinc
  • KSP1 was a K1 compiler plugin; KSP2 uses the Kotlin Analysis API and is the default since KSP 2.0.0 (early 2025). KSP1 is deprecated and incompatible with Kotlin 2.3+. ksp.useKSP2=false was the escape hatch while it existed.
  • KSP processes incrementally with "isolating" vs "aggregating" outputs declared by processors.
  • A module running both KAPT and KSP pays for both. The win only appears when the module has zero KAPT processors.
  • Processors that are KAPT-only (some older libraries, data binding) keep KAPT alive. Data binding still requires kapt in some setups; check AGP docs for your version.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
plugins {
    id("com.google.devtools.ksp")   // version must match your Kotlin line, e.g. 2.x.y-z
}
dependencies {
    implementation(libs.room.runtime)
    ksp(libs.room.compiler)          // was: kapt(libs.room.compiler)
    ksp(libs.hilt.compiler)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Migrating one processor and leaving the kapt plugin applied with nothing else to process; it still runs stub generation in some configurations.
  • Mixing processors that depend on each other's output across KAPT and KSP (e.g. Hilt needing Dagger output generated by the other tool).
  • Using an old KSP version that does not match the Kotlin compiler.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are Java stubs slow? → They're a full extra compile-like pass producing Java source for every Kotlin class, even unchanged ones in some cases.
  2. Can KSP modify existing code? → No; like APT it only generates new files. Modifying code needs a compiler plugin.
  3. How do you verify the win? → Gradle build scan or --profile, compare kaptGenerateStubs* + kapt* tasks before vs ksp* tasks after, on clean and incremental builds.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "KSP is faster". The senior explains stubs, KSP1 vs KSP2, the "all or nothing per module" rule, and how to measure.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: In mixed modules the KAPT stub task routinely dominates incremental builds after a one-line Kotlin change; removing the last kapt processor is where the incremental build time drops.

questions.subtopic: Java caller passes null into Kotlin
questions.contextHtml:
A payments app (1.2M DAU, ~35% legacy Java code) moved PaymentFormatter from Java to Kotlin in release 8.14. Crash-free users dropped from 99.6% to 99.1% within a day. Crashlytics top issue (11k events):

java.lang.NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: method com.pay.ui.PaymentFormatter.formatAmount, parameter currencyCode
    at com.pay.ui.PaymentFormatter.formatAmount(PaymentFormatter.kt)
    at com.pay.legacy.ReceiptActivity.bindHeader(ReceiptActivity.java:212)
    at com.pay.legacy.ReceiptActivity.onCreate(ReceiptActivity.java:98)

Kotlin signature: fun formatAmount(amountMinor: Long, currencyCode: String): String. The Java side reads currencyCode from getIntent().getStringExtra("currency"). Crashes cluster on receipts opened from push notifications (deep links built by a server template). The previous Java version of formatAmount "handled null" by printing an empty currency. Also noticed: a spike of ANR reports on the same release (red herring: from an unrelated image-loading change).
questions.promptHtml: What happened, how do you stop the crash today, and how do you make this class of bug unlikely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the parameter String?" or "add !! checks on the Java side". Doesn't explain why Kotlin crashes at entry, doesn't find the real source (push intents without the extra), and has no plan for other Java-to-Kotlin boundaries.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Are all crashes from the push entry point? (confirms data source)
    • Did the push template or backend change recently? (two-sided change)
    • What did old receipts look like for these users: empty currency, or wrong? (decides correct behavior)
    • How many other Java callers hit newly converted Kotlin APIs this release? (blast radius)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that makes ReceiptActivity handle a missing extra (default to the account currency from the payment record, log a non-fatal). If a server-side flag can re-enable the old receipt path or fix the push template, do it in parallel; it fixes users without an app update. Halt staged rollout of 8.14 at its current percentage.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • Push-built intents omit currency; Java passes null; Kotlin rejects it at entry. Fits the stack and clustering.
    • A Java caller passes a nullable value from another source (saved state after process death). Check other stacks.
    • Kotlin compiler change in this release caused it. Unlikely; checks existed before, the class was just Java.
  4. How I'd verify each: Crashlytics custom keys / breadcrumbs for launch source; reproduce with adb shell am start -n com.pay/.legacy.ReceiptActivity without the extra; decompile PaymentFormatter (Show Kotlin Bytecode) to see Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter(currencyCode, "currencyCode") as the first instruction; inspect server push template history.
  5. Root cause: Kotlin inserts a null check at the start of every public function for non-null reference parameters, because Java callers are not checked by the compiler. Java's getStringExtra returns a platform/@Nullable value; Java code passed it straight through. Previously the Java formatter tolerated null, so the missing extra was invisible. The conversion changed the contract from "accepts null" to "requires non-null", and the boundary enforced it loudly.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: validate at the boundary where the null originates (the Activity), with a real default:
    String currency = getIntent().getStringExtra("currency");
if (currency == null) {
    currency = payment.getCurrencyCode();   // source of truth
    Log.w(TAG, "receipt opened without currency extra");
}
header.setText(formatter.formatAmount(payment.getAmountMinor(), currency));
    • Long-term: when converting Java APIs that Java still calls, keep the old null tolerance only if it was a real contract (then use String? and handle it explicitly in Kotlin). Otherwise keep non-null and fix callers. Add @NonNull/@Nullable (androidx.annotation) to the remaining Java code around boundaries so the Kotlin side sees real types, and so Android Lint/IDE flags Java passing a nullable into non-null. Fix the push template so currency is always present.
  7. Prevention: A conversion checklist ("list Java callers; for each parameter, can it be null today?"); Lint UnknownNullness enabled on Java modules being migrated; unit/instrumentation test for opening the receipt from a push intent; Crashlytics alert on new "Parameter specified as non-null" signatures per release.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not disable the checks with -Xno-param-assertions: it moves the NPE deeper and makes it harder to debug. I would not blanket-change parameters to nullable "to be safe"; that spreads nullability through Kotlin code. I'd not chase the ANR spike here; separate stacks and timing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the Kotlin function were internal or private? → No parameter check is emitted for private functions; for internal it still is (it's public in bytecode). A null would surface later as an NPE on first use instead.
  • Why didn't the Java compiler warn? → getStringExtra is annotated nullable but the Java caller didn't use a nullness checker; Kotlin's String maps to @NotNull in metadata/annotations, which IDE inspections can flag if enabled.
  • Would requireNotNull in Kotlin be better? → It gives a clearer message, but the real fix is the caller's data.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: On a migration of ~200 Java classes, we generated a list of every Kotlin public function called from Java and audited parameters marked non-null. We found nine places where Java passed values that could be null after process death; fixing them before release avoided a repeat of exactly this crash.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: makes the param nullable or adds !!, cannot explain the crash message.
  • Hire: explains Kotlin's entry-point null checks and fixes the caller with a sensible default.
  • Strong hire: also traces the null to the push template, separates the red herring, and installs annotations/lint/tests to protect remaining boundaries.

questions.contextHtml:
A design-system team converted PrimaryButton from Java to Kotlin. After the release, buttons in dark mode and on two OEM skins lost their ripple, padding and text appearance; on most Pixels they looked fine in light mode. No crashes. The Kotlin code:

class PrimaryButton @JvmOverloads constructor(
    context: Context,
    attrs: AttributeSet? = null,
    defStyleAttr: Int = 0
) : AppCompatButton(context, attrs, defStyleAttr) {
    init {
        context.obtainStyledAttributes(attrs, R.styleable.PrimaryButton, defStyleAttr, 0).use { a ->
            cornerRadius = a.getDimension(R.styleable.PrimaryButton_cornerRadius, 0f)
        }
    }
    var cornerRadius = 0f
}

The old Java class had three constructors, the 2-arg one calling super(context, attrs). Red herring: the release also bumped Material Components by a patch version.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs, explain why they only show on some themes/devices, and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Material update broke styles" or "@JvmOverloads is fine, it's the same as three constructors". Misses that the generated 2-arg constructor passes defStyleAttr = 0, bypassing the theme's default button style.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the theme set buttonStyle or materialButtonStyle differently per night/OEM overlay? Are the broken buttons inflated from XML (2-arg constructor)? Did the Java version call super(context, attrs) in the 2-arg constructor?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident with crashes; ship the fix in the next release, or set style="@style/Widget.App.Button" explicitly on the most visible screens as a stopgap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • defStyleAttr = 0 default: XML inflation calls the 2-arg constructor; @JvmOverloads generates PrimaryButton(Context, AttributeSet) that calls the 3-arg one with 0. Old Java called super(context, attrs), which internally uses R.attr.buttonStyle. With 0, the theme's default button style isn't applied. Themes that rely on buttonStyle (dark theme overlay, OEM themes) lose ripple/padding; light theme may still look acceptable if the style's values match the widget defaults.
    • Initialization order bug: var cornerRadius = 0f is declared after init, so the property initializer runs after the init block and resets the value read from XML to 0. Corner radius from XML is silently lost everywhere.
    • Material patch update: possible, but the symptom matches the style resolution path, and reverting the button conversion in a test build is a fast check.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector: compare resolved attributes (background, padding, textAppearance) and where they come from; set breakpoints in the 2-arg constructor; decompile to see the generated constructor passing 0; screenshot tests (Paparazzi/Roborazzi) for light/dark before and after.
  5. Root cause: @JvmOverloads fills omitted args with Kotlin defaults; it does not replicate per-constructor super calls. The View framework expects defStyleAttr to be the theme attribute for the default style. Separately, Kotlin runs property initializers and init blocks in declaration order.
  6. Fix:
class PrimaryButton @JvmOverloads constructor(
    context: Context,
    attrs: AttributeSet? = null,
    defStyleAttr: Int = androidx.appcompat.R.attr.buttonStyle   // what AppCompatButton(context, attrs) uses
) : AppCompatButton(context, attrs, defStyleAttr) {

    var cornerRadius = 0f          // declared before init so init's assignment survives

    init {
        context.obtainStyledAttributes(attrs, R.styleable.PrimaryButton, defStyleAttr, 0).use { a ->
            cornerRadius = a.getDimension(R.styleable.PrimaryButton_cornerRadius, 0f)
        }
    }
}

Or write explicit secondary constructors that each call the matching super(...), which is safest when the parent's default style attr is not public or differs per API. 7. Prevention: Screenshot tests in light/dark and font scale for design-system components; a review checklist item: "custom View with @JvmOverloads: what does defStyleAttr default to?"; a detekt rule or custom lint flagging defStyleAttr: Int = 0 in View subclasses. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not hardcode style values in code to "fix" the look; it breaks theming. I wouldn't drop @JvmOverloads everywhere; it's fine when the default is the right attr.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is obtainStyledAttributes(...).use {} valid? → TypedArray implements AutoCloseable from API 31; on lower APIs use the core-ktx use extension or recycle() explicitly. Check your minSdk.
  • Which constructor does XML inflation call? → The 2-arg (Context, AttributeSet) one.
  • What if the parent is a MaterialButton? → Use its own default attr (materialButtonStyle); otherwise Material theming is lost the same way.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A design-system library lost elevation on all its cards in dark mode after a Kotlin conversion; the culprit was one defStyleAttr = 0 default copied across eight components. Screenshot tests would have caught it on the PR.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the library update, can't explain constructor generation.
  • Hire: finds the defStyleAttr = 0 issue and fixes it.
  • Strong hire: also catches the init-order bug, explains why only some themes are affected, and adds screenshot tests/lint.

questions.contextHtml:
A 140-module app (Kotlin 1.9.24, Compose compiler 1.5.14, KAPT for Room/Hilt/Glide/data binding, KSP1 for Moshi) must move to Kotlin 2.x this quarter because a new library needs it. Weekly releases cannot pause; 60 engineers merge ~150 PRs/day. First attempt on a branch (kotlin = 2.0.21) fails:

e: This version (1.5.14) of the Compose Compiler requires Kotlin version 1.9.24 but you appear to be using Kotlin version 2.0.21
w: Kapt currently doesn't support language version 2.0+. Falling back to 1.9.
e: file:///.../CheckoutReducer.kt:88:21 Smart cast to 'Loaded' is impossible, because 'state' is a mutable property that could have been changed by this time
e: Unresolved reference: JvmDefault   (legacy module)
detekt: Unsupported Kotlin version, crashes on parsing

Red herring: Gradle configuration cache warnings that also appeared on the branch (they existed on main too).
questions.promptHtml: Plan and execute this migration without freezing development.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Bump the version, fix the errors, merge the big PR." A long-lived branch with 140 modules of fixes conflicts daily, and there's no rollback plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Which target version? Going straight to the latest 2.x avoids two migrations; I'd check AGP, KSP and Compose BOM compatibility for that version.
    • Which tools parse Kotlin (detekt, ktlint, Lint, custom compiler plugins, Anvil, Paparazzi)? Each has a minimum version for 2.x.
    • Do we publish libraries to other teams who compile with older Kotlin? (Metadata forward-compat.)
    • What's the CI time budget and baseline build times? (to prove we didn't regress)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident. Keep main on 1.9 and make every fix land on main as a backward-compatible PR: code that compiles on both K1 and K2.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (blocker categories):
    • Compose compiler coupling: on 2.0+ replace composeOptions { kotlinCompilerExtensionVersion } with the org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose plugin at the Kotlin version. Mechanical, done in the switch PR.
    • Real source errors from K2 (smart-cast stability, resolution changes, removed deprecated APIs like @JvmDefault). Fixable on main beforehand.
    • Tooling: detekt/ktlint/Lint/KSP versions. Upgrade those on main first where they support both.
