    • KAPT on K2: in 2.0 it fell back to K1 stubs; K2 kapt is default from 2.1.20. Plan to move Room/Hilt/Glide to KSP, keep data binding on kapt if required.
    • Configuration cache warnings: pre-existing, ignore for this project.
  4. How I'd verify each: A nightly CI job building main with a Gradle property override -Pkotlin.version=2.x (version catalog reads it), producing an error count trend; kotlin.build.report.output=file for compile timings; full unit/screenshot test suite on the K2 job; Macrobenchmark for startup to catch codegen changes (e.g. invokedynamic lambdas).
  5. Root cause: Kotlin 2.0 replaced the compiler frontend; compiler plugins and code relying on K1-specific behavior or unsound smart casts break. The Compose compiler was version-locked to Kotlin before 2.0.
  6. Fix (the plan):
    • Phase 0 (week 1): upgrade detekt/ktlint/KSP/AGP to versions supporting both 1.9 and 2.x; add the nightly K2 job.
    • Phase 1 (weeks 1-3): fix K2 errors on main in small PRs owned by module owners, e.g. capturing mutable properties into a local val before when:
    // before: if (state is Loaded) render(state.items)   // state is a var property
val s = state
if (s is Loaded) render(s.items)
    Remove @JvmDefault usage (use -jvm-default/-Xjvm-default modes). Move KAPT processors to KSP module by module.
    • Phase 2: a single switch PR: version bump + Compose plugin + flag cleanup, merged early in a release cycle, behind a quick revert path (one commit).
    • Phase 3: monitor crash-free rate, ANR, startup p50/p95, APK size for 2 releases; then remove the dual-compat hacks and turn on new language features.
  7. Prevention: Keep the "next Kotlin" CI job permanently so future upgrades are small; treat warnings from the compiler about deprecated features as errors in CI (allWarningsAsErrors for selected modules).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): No long-lived migration branch. No suppressing K2 errors with casts (as Loaded) that hide real races. I would not combine the Kotlin bump with a large AGP major upgrade in the same PR; one variable at a time so a regression is attributable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A library you depend on was compiled with Kotlin 2.2 and you're on 1.9. → The 1.9 compiler may refuse to read newer metadata ("compiled with an incompatible version"); this forces upgrade order or an older library version.
  • Release build size grew 2% after the switch. → Compare dex with APK Analyzer; check new codegen defaults and kept kotlin-reflect, verify R8 config.
  • Can you upgrade Kotlin in some modules only? → Not practically: one Kotlin Gradle plugin version per build. You can set languageVersion per module (where still supported) for gradual language changes, not compiler versions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: We ran the "next Kotlin" nightly for six weeks before the switch. The error count went from ~400 to 0 through 70 small PRs, and the actual switch PR was 30 lines and was reverted once (a KSP version mismatch), then re-landed the same day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang branch, no awareness of Compose compiler coupling or KAPT.
  • Hire: categorizes errors, fixes forward-compatible on main, knows Compose plugin change.
  • Strong hire: nightly K2 CI, phased plan with rollback, KAPT→KSP, tooling versions, post-switch metrics and metadata compatibility.

questions.contextHtml: A food delivery app (8M MAU, 60% of users on devices with <= 4 GB RAM) sees cold-start p95 regress from 1.9 s to 2.25 s over three releases. A Perfetto trace of Application.onCreate on a low-end device shows a 210 ms block in RemoteConfigRepository.init with frames in kotlin.reflect.jvm.internal.KClassImpl, ReflectionFactoryImpl, com.squareup.moshi.kotlin.reflect.KotlinJsonAdapterFactory. The repository parses a 40-model config JSON with Moshi.Builder().add(KotlinJsonAdapterFactory()). APK size also grew ~1.1 MB when moshi-kotlin was added. Red herrings: a new analytics SDK initialized in onCreate (trace shows 18 ms), and GC events that track overall allocation.
questions.promptHtml: What's happening and how do you get the startup time back?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move parsing to a background thread." It hides the main-thread time but keeps the cost, the APK size, and doesn't explain why reflection is slow.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the config needed before the first frame? Which models use reflective adapters vs generated ones? Is the R8 config keeping all of kotlin-reflect? Do we have a startup Macrobenchmark in CI?
  2. Immediate mitigation: If the config isn't required for the first frame, move its parse off the critical path (lazy on first use, or a background coroutine with the cached last-known config served synchronously). This is a stopgap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • Full Kotlin reflection: KotlinJsonAdapterFactory uses kotlin-reflect to find primary constructors, parameter names, defaults and nullability by parsing @Metadata for each class. First-time costs: loading kotlin-reflect classes, building descriptors per model. 40 models on a slow CPU explains 200 ms.
    • Classloading/dex verification of the newly added kotlin-reflect code on first launch after install/update. Contributes, measured separately via the trace's class-loading slices.
    • Analytics SDK: 18 ms, not the main driver.
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto with Trace.beginSection("config-parse"); Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric cold start with and without the reflective factory; APK Analyzer to check kotlin/reflect/jvm/internal package size in the dex; method tracing in the Android Studio CPU profiler for the parse.
  5. Root cause: Runtime reflection over Kotlin metadata on the main thread during startup. Kotlin-specific information is not in normal Java reflection, so kotlin-reflect parses protobuf metadata and builds a large model per class the first time.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: switch these models to Moshi codegen via KSP (@JsonClass(generateAdapter = true)), drop KotlinJsonAdapterFactory, and remove the kotlin-reflect dependency if nothing else needs it.
    @com.squareup.moshi.JsonClass(generateAdapter = true)
data class FeatureFlags(val newCheckout: Boolean = false, val maxCartItems: Int = 50)

val moshi = com.squareup.moshi.Moshi.Builder().build()  // no KotlinJsonAdapterFactory
    • Long-term: move models to kotlinx.serialization if the codebase is standardizing; add a Baseline Profile covering startup; cache parsed config.
  7. Prevention: Startup Macrobenchmark in CI with a regression threshold (e.g. +5% p50 fails the build); dependency guard (e.g. a Gradle task that fails if kotlin-reflect appears in the release runtime classpath without approval); review checklist for "reflection on startup path".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Not just backgrounding the parse: still burns CPU during startup competing with the first frame, and the APK size stays. Not hand-writing adapters for 40 models: codegen gives the same speed with less maintenance. Not removing R8 rules blindly to save size: reflective code would break.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• After switching, release builds throw "Cannot find adapter" for one model. → Missing @JsonClass(generateAdapter = true) or R8 stripped the generated adapter; Moshi's codegen ships keep rules, check they're applied and the annotation is present.
  • Product says the config must be applied before the first frame. → Serve the cached version synchronously from disk (tiny generated-adapter parse), refresh in background.
  • Is Foo::class.java also slow? → No, that's a Java Class reference; only full kotlin-reflect APIs pay this cost.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Removing a single reflective adapter factory cut ~150 ms from p95 cold start on low-end devices and 900 KB from the APK; a one-line dependency guard has kept kotlin-reflect out since.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: backgrounding only; can't explain why reflection is slow.
  • Hire: identifies kotlin-reflect via the trace and moves to codegen.
  • Strong hire: explains metadata parsing, measures with Macrobenchmark/Perfetto, separates red herrings, adds CI guards and startup budget.

questions.subtopic: Checked exceptions across a Java proxy
questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review. A banking app's Java "resilience" layer wraps Kotlin repository interfaces in java.lang.reflect.Proxy to add logging and retries. Kotlin interface:

interface StatementRepository { fun download(month: YearMonth): File }

The Kotlin implementation throws IOException on network failure. The Java retry handler only retries IOException:

} catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); }  // inside InvocationHandler
...
try { repo.download(m); } catch (UndeclaredThrowableException | RuntimeException e) { showGenericError(); }

During a 40-minute backend degradation, retries never fired: 92k users saw "Something went wrong" instead of a transparent retry; support tickets up 6x. Logs: java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException ... Caused by: java.io.IOException: unexpected end of stream. Red herring: OkHttp connection pool warnings in the same window.
questions.promptHtml: Walk through the review: root cause, fix, and what you'd change process-wise.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "OkHttp had connection issues." Or "catch Exception everywhere". Doesn't explain why the exception type changed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: When was StatementRepository converted to Kotlin? Did the retry path ever work in production or only in Java unit tests? Which other interfaces go through the proxy?
  2. Immediate mitigation (already done during incident, review it): Backend recovered; a hotfix should make the handler unwrap UndeclaredThrowableException to its cause until signatures are fixed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • Undeclared checked exception: the Kotlin interface method has no throws IOException, so the proxy wraps it in UndeclaredThrowableException. The retry logic never sees IOException.
    • Retry policy misconfigured: possible, but logs show the wrapped type.
    • OkHttp pool warnings: symptom of the backend degradation, not of the missing retry.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test that builds the proxy over a fake Kotlin implementation throwing IOException and asserts the caught type; javap on the interface to confirm no Exceptions attribute on download; git blame for the Java-to-Kotlin conversion date.
  5. Root cause: Proxy follows Java's contract: if the handler throws a checked exception not declared by the interface method, it is wrapped in UndeclaredThrowableException. Kotlin omitted the throws clause because Kotlin has no checked exceptions. When the interface was converted from Java (where it declared throws IOException), the JVM signature lost it.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: @Throws(IOException::class) on the interface method, restoring the old JVM signature:
    interface StatementRepository {
    @Throws(java.io.IOException::class)
    fun download(month: java.time.YearMonth): java.io.File
}
    • Long-term: replace the reflective Java proxy with explicit Kotlin decorators (class RetryingStatementRepository(private val delegate: StatementRepository) : StatementRepository by delegate) or move retries to the network layer (OkHttp interceptor or coroutine retry with backoff); make errors typed (sealed result) so retry policy doesn't depend on exception classes.
  7. Prevention: Conversion checklist: "does any Java code catch checked exceptions from this API or proxy it?"; a contract test for every proxied interface; alert on UndeclaredThrowableException in logs/Crashlytics non-fatals.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Not catching Throwable and retrying everything: you would retry programmer errors and cancellation. Not blaming the backend in the review: the client's retry was the safety net that failed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would this happen with a suspend function through the proxy? → Suspend functions through Java proxies are messy anyway (Continuation param, COROUTINE_SUSPENDED); don't proxy them reflectively.
  • Does Mockito/MockK hit this? → Mocks configured to throw a checked exception not declared by the method: Mockito rejects it as "Checked exception is invalid for this method"; @Throws fixes it too.
  • Where else does the missing throws clause matter? → Java callers can't catch (IOException) at all (compile error), which pushes them to broad catches.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A similar review found five proxied interfaces converted to Kotlin over a year; all had silently lost retry behavior. The fix took an hour; the contract tests are what stopped it recurring.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:

questions.contextHtml:
A ride-hailing app (3M DAU) passes a Trip between screens in a Bundle. Crashlytics shows 0.4% of sessions with IllegalStateException: Trip.driverName not set after returning from the background (process death restore) and a few users seeing a blank fare after rotating the screen on the payment page. Code:

@Parcelize
class Trip(val id: String, val pickup: String) : Parcelable {
    var driverName: String? = null
    var fareMinor: Long = 0L
    @IgnoredOnParcel var cachedMap: Bitmap? = null
}

// Warning in build output, ignored by the team:
// w: Trip.kt: Property would not be serialized into a Parcel. Add '@IgnoredOnParcel' annotation to remove this warning

driverName and fareMinor are set after the trip is assigned. Red herring: a recent Navigation library upgrade.
questions.promptHtml: Why are those values lost, and how do you fix it and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Parcelable is broken on rotation; use a ViewModel" or "bump Navigation". Misses that only primary-constructor properties are written to the Parcel.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the loss only occur after process death or recreation (anything that round-trips a Parcel)? Where are driverName/fareMinor assigned? Do we have the build warning in CI logs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: move the fields into the primary constructor, and re-fetch the trip by id if a restored Trip has missing data.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • Body properties aren't parcelled: the Parcelize plugin only serializes properties declared in the primary constructor. The warning text says exactly this.
    • Navigation/Bundle bug: unlikely, since id and pickup survive.
    • Concurrency or a stale reference: possible but wouldn't explain process-death-only crashes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test: write to Parcel.obtain(), setDataPosition(0), read back via Trip.CREATOR, assert all fields (Robolectric or instrumentation); "Don't keep activities" developer option to reproduce; adb shell am kill for process death; grep CI logs for the Parcelize warning.
  5. Root cause: Parcelize generates writeToParcel and createFromParcel from the primary constructor parameters, because a restore must be able to call the constructor. Properties in the class body get default values on restore (null and 0). The object in memory looked fine; the copy that came back through the Bundle didn't.
  6. Fix:
@Parcelize
data class Trip(
    val id: String,
    val pickup: String,
    val driverName: String? = null,
    val fareMinor: Long = 0L,
) : Parcelable
// Bitmap does not belong in a Parcelable at all: keep it in a cache keyed by id.

Update state with copy() and store the new instance. Treat any Bundle payload as small (the Binder transaction buffer is about 1 MB shared per process; TransactionTooLargeException beyond that), so passing an id and loading from a repository is often better. 7. Prevention: Treat the Parcelize warning as an error (allWarningsAsErrors or a targeted -Werror for it); unit test round trip for each parcelable model; code review rule "Parcelable classes are immutable data classes". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not hand-write writeToParcel; it reintroduces the boilerplate bugs. I would not add @IgnoredOnParcel to silence the warning without checking whether the data is needed after restore.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if a property in the primary constructor is a non-Parcelable class? → Compile error unless you supply a Parceler/@TypeParceler, or the type is Serializable or a supported collection.
  • Is @Parcelize Experimental? → No, it's a stable Kotlin plugin (kotlin-parcelize); the old kotlin-android-extensions version was deprecated.
  • Why not just Serializable? → Slower reflection-based path and larger payloads; Parcelable is the Android IPC format.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "works on my phone" bug lived for months because developers never killed the process. Adding one Parcel round-trip test per model found three more silently dropped fields.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames Navigation; can't reproduce process death.
  • Hire: knows only primary-constructor properties are parcelled and fixes it.
  • Strong hire: adds round-trip tests, warns about Bundle size/Bitmap, and enforces the warning in CI.

questions.contextHtml: A 90-module Android app has clean builds at 14 minutes and incremental (one-line change in a leaf Kotlin file) at 3 min 40 s on CI-class laptops. A build scan shows the top tasks: :feature:*:kaptGenerateStubsDebugKotlin and :feature:*:kaptDebugKotlin totalling about 41% of CPU time. Processors in use: Hilt (Dagger), Room, Glide, Moshi codegen (already KSP), and data binding in 6 legacy modules. Kotlin 2.2.x, AGP 8.x. Management asks for a plan to cut incremental builds by 40%. Red herring: the team wants to enable the Gradle remote cache first.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do, in what order, and how do you show it worked?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch everything to KSP" with no sequencing; or "add more CI machines". Doesn't know a module still applying kapt pays stub generation, and doesn't plan for libraries that lack KSP support.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which modules actually use which processors? Which libraries in use lack KSP support (check versions)? Is kapt.use.k2 at default? Is the configuration cache enabled? What is the baseline per task on a recent main?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cheap wins first: enable build cache and configuration cache if not on, ksp.incremental default is on, kapt.incremental.apt=true and kapt.use.worker.api=true (defaults in recent Kotlin; verify), org.gradle.parallel=true. Not a fix, but visible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • KAPT stubs: every kapt module re-generates Java stubs for all its Kotlin classes after any change in it or its dependencies' ABI.
    • A few giant modules with Hilt aggregation dominate the critical path, so reducing module count in the path matters more than average speed.
    • Remote cache wouldn't help incremental local edits much, since the changed module still re-runs.
  4. How I'd verify each: Gradle build scan with task timing and critical path; --profile; -Pkotlin.build.report.output=file for Kotlin task breakdown; Android Studio Build Analyzer; compare before/after on the same machine with a scripted "touch a leaf file" benchmark (Gradle Profiler).
  5. Root cause: KAPT converts Kotlin to Java stubs and runs javac annotation processing. It is in maintenance mode and its cost scales with code in each kapt module. KSP reads Kotlin directly and is incremental with "isolating" vs "aggregating" processors.
  6. Fix:
    • Migrate in order of impact: Room (ksp(libs.room.compiler); Room supports KSP) → Glide (KSP supported) → Hilt/Dagger (ksp(libs.hilt.compiler); verify your Hilt version's KSP support and its known limits) → remaining.
    • Per module, remove the kotlin-kapt plugin entirely once its last kapt dependency is gone; a module running both pays both.
    • Keep data binding on kapt where required, but isolate those modules and plan to migrate the 6 legacy screens to view binding/Compose over time.
    plugins { id("com.google.devtools.ksp") }   // KSP2 default, version aligned to Kotlin
dependencies {
    ksp(libs.room.compiler)
    ksp(libs.hilt.compiler)
}
    • Split a monster Hilt-aggregating module so a change doesn't re-run aggregation for everything.
  7. Prevention: CI job that fails when a new module applies kapt without approval; dashboard of the top 10 slowest tasks per week; keep KSP and Kotlin versions aligned by catalog.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I'd not migrate all processors in one PR (mixed outputs across KAPT/KSP can break Hilt aggregation and are hard to bisect). I'd not rely on remote cache to fix incremental builds. I'd not claim "40% faster" before measuring: expected gains are bounded by the 41% of CPU time kapt represents, and CPU time isn't wall-clock on the critical path.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• After migration, incremental time dropped only 15%. → Critical path is elsewhere (e.g. dexing, resource merging, a monolithic :app), look at the scan's critical path, not total CPU time.
  • Hilt compile fails with "cannot find symbol" for a generated class. → Generated sources across mixed processors or a stale KSP/Hilt version mismatch; check versions and that kapt isn't also generating the same sources.
  • Is KAPT removed in Kotlin 2.x? → No, it's still available (K2 mode default since 2.1.20), only in maintenance; but KSP1 is the thing that stopped working with 2.3+.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving Room and Hilt to KSP across 60 modules, then deleting 52 kapt plugin applications, took incremental builds from 3:40 to 2:05; the long pole turned out to be one aggregating module we split afterwards.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "just use KSP", no measurement, suggests more hardware.
  • Hire: explains stubs vs direct symbol access, migrates in sensible order, measures with a build scan.
  • Strong hire: critical-path thinking, per-module kapt removal, handles data-binding holdouts, and sets guard rails.

questions.subtopic: Designing a Kotlin library API for Java consumers
questions.contextHtml:
Your team owns sdk-core, a Kotlin SDK distributed as an AAR to 14 partner apps; roughly half are still Java, and three partners are on Java 8 with no Kotlin stdlib of their own. The v1 API:

class SdkClient(val config: Config) {
    companion object { fun create(ctx: Context, apiKey: String, env: Env = Env.PROD, timeoutMs: Int = 30_000): SdkClient }
    suspend fun fetchProfile(id: String): Profile
    fun events(): Flow<SdkEvent>
    fun <T> run(block: Session.() -> T): T
}
data class Profile(val id: String, val name: String, val tier: Tier = Tier.FREE)
enum class Env { PROD, STAGING }

Partner tickets: "cannot call fetchProfile from Java", "SdkClient.Companion.create everywhere", "adding a field to Profile broke our build", "NoSuchMethodError after your 1.3 release". Binary compatibility is a stated promise (semver).
questions.promptHtml: Redesign the public API surface and the release process so it works for Java partners without wrecking the Kotlin API.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just add @JvmStatic and @JvmOverloads everywhere." That ignores suspend/Flow from Java, data class evolution, and the NoSuchMethodError category.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which Java partners can use Kotlin coroutines transitively? Do we have API usage stats per method? Are we allowed a v2 major? Minimum Java/desugaring level? Who pays for the support cost, us or the partners?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add the binary-compatibility-validator (apiCheck) to CI immediately to stop new breaks; publish a 1.3.1 restoring removed signatures (e.g. keep old create(Context, String) overloads). Document supported entry points.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (sources of pain):
    • Signature changes by adding default params: changes the JVM method descriptor, NoSuchMethodError for compiled callers.
    • data class in public API: copy() and componentN() signatures change whenever a property is added, so it's binary-incompatible by design.
    • suspend and Flow: Java sees Object fetchProfile(String, Continuation<? super Profile>).
    • Companion and lambda-with-receiver entry points: ugly or unusable from Java.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run apiDump diff between 1.2 and 1.3; write a Java sample module that compiles against the API as a living test; javap on public classes.
  5. Root cause: Kotlin features (defaults, data classes, suspend, receivers) compile to JVM shapes that are fragile or unusable for Java and for binary evolution. The API was designed for Kotlin source compatibility only.
  6. Fix:
    • Static entry with a builder; keep create(...) overloads explicit rather than via defaults:
    class SdkClient private constructor(private val config: Config) {
    class Builder(private val ctx: Context, private val apiKey: String) {
        private var env = Env.PROD
        private var timeoutMs = 30_000
        fun env(e: Env) = apply { env = e }
        fun timeoutMs(ms: Int) = apply { timeoutMs = ms }
        fun build(): SdkClient = SdkClient(Config(ctx.applicationContext, apiKey, env, timeoutMs))
    }
    // Kotlin-friendly:
    suspend fun fetchProfile(id: String): Profile = TODO()
    // Java-friendly: callback + cancellable handle, or CompletableFuture/ListenableFuture
    fun fetchProfileAsync(id: String, cb: Callback<Profile>): Cancellable = TODO()
}
    • Profile: a regular class (class Profile internal constructor(...) with vals, equals/hashCode/toString hand-written or generated), no copy; add a toBuilder() if needed.
    • Flow: expose events() for Kotlin and an addListener/removeListener or Publisher-style API for Java (kotlinx-coroutines-reactive). Mark rarely-used Kotlin-only things @JvmSynthetic to hide them from Java.
    • Use @JvmStatic, @JvmOverloads only on frozen, intentional signatures; use @Throws where Java should catch; use @file:JvmName.
    • Explicit API mode (kotlin { explicitApi() }) so nothing becomes public by accident; @RequiresOptIn for experimental surface.
    • Kotlin 2.4 added the experimental @IntroducedAt to keep binary compat when adding optional params; evaluate it only once stable, not for a published API now.
  7. Prevention: apiCheck in CI gating merges; Java sample app compiled in CI; deprecation cycle (@Deprecated(level = WARNING) for a minor, ERROR next, remove in next major); published changelog with binary-compat notes; shade or document the Kotlin stdlib/coroutines versions you require.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I'd not write the SDK in Java just for partners; the Kotlin API stays idiomatic with a thin Java-friendly layer. I wouldn't use data classes for anything partners can construct or compare long-term. I wouldn't promise suspend-from-Java compatibility; it's an implementation detail of Continuation passing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A partner on Java 8 sees NoClassDefFoundError: kotlin/jvm/internal/Intrinsics. → They exclude the Kotlin stdlib; declare it as an api dependency in your POM/Gradle metadata, or shade.
  • Should the Profile be a @JvmRecord? → Only if all consumers support Java 16+ bytecode; most Android partners don't, so no.
  • How to evolve Tier enum? → Adding enum entries breaks exhaustive when in Kotlin consumers; consider a sealed/class-with-constants pattern with an UNKNOWN value for forward compatibility.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single "harmless" added default parameter in a patch release crashed 11% of a partner's sessions on launch with NoSuchMethodError; the post-incident change was apiCheck on every PR and a Java sample module that must compile.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sprinkles annotations, no compatibility process.
  • Hire: identifies defaults/data class/suspend problems and proposes builders, overloads, a Java-facing async API.
  • Strong hire: adds API dump gating, explicit API mode, deprecation policy, stdlib packaging, enum/data class evolution, and keeps the Kotlin API idiomatic.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app (900k DAU) finished migrating from Gson to kotlinx.serialization (Kotlin 2.2, plugin applied). Next morning: support reports that "Save payee" silently saves with country = null for 3% of users, and crash rate rises 0.3% with:

kotlinx.serialization.MissingFieldException: Fields [ledgerId] are required for type with serial name 'com.fin.api.AccountDto', but they were missing at path: $.accounts[2]

Models:

@Serializable data class PayeeRequest(val name: String, val iban: String, val country: String = "IN", val isFavorite: Boolean = false)
@Serializable data class AccountDto(val id: String, val ledgerId: String, val balanceMinor: Long)
val json = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }

The backend treats an absent country as "use user's profile country" (null), but the app previously (Gson) always sent country: null when unset. Some accounts from a legacy backend shard never include ledgerId. Red herring: a CDN certificate rotation that morning.
questions.promptHtml: Explain both failures and the safest rollout from here.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add ignoreUnknownKeys" (already there) or "make everything nullable". Doesn't notice encodeDefaults and that Gson tolerated missing data by lying about non-null.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the backend contract say ledgerId is required, and which shard omits it? What did the request body look like before vs after (capture with a proxy)? Is the migration behind a flag? What's the oldest app version still receiving responses with missing fields?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the percentage via staged rollout / kill-switch flag to the Gson path if one exists; otherwise a hotfix. For the crash: tolerate the missing field with a default or a nullable type plus a repository-level fallback. For the request: set encoding behavior explicitly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • Two different mechanisms. (a) Request: Json default encodeDefaults = false omits properties equal to their defaults, so country = "IN" isn't sent when the user didn't change it, and the server maps absence to profile country instead. Previously the key was always present. (b) Response: ledgerId is non-null with no default; kotlinx.serialization throws on missing fields, where Gson left a null in a non-null Kotlin property that later never crashed because nothing used it.
    • CDN certificate rotation: would show as SSL exceptions, not MissingFieldException; ignore.
  4. How I'd verify each: Charles/mitmproxy or OkHttp HttpLoggingInterceptor to compare request bodies old vs new build; raw response samples from the failing shard; unit tests with captured JSON fixtures; Crashlytics custom key with accounts shard id.
  5. Root cause: Behavior differences, not a library bug: Gson reflected fields and did not run constructors or enforce nullability; kotlinx.serialization uses generated serializers that honor Kotlin constructors, defaults and non-null types, and by default doesn't encode default values.
  6. Fix: 
    val json = Json {
    ignoreUnknownKeys = true
    encodeDefaults = true            // send "country":"IN" even when default
    explicitNulls = false            // don't send nulls the API treats as absent (decide per contract)
    coerceInputValues = true         // null/unknown enum -> default where a default exists
}

@Serializable
data class AccountDto(val id: String, val ledgerId: String? = null, val balanceMinor: Long) // model reality
    Or annotate a single field with @EncodeDefault instead of changing the global setting. Map AccountDto to a domain model where a missing ledgerId is handled explicitly (e.g. fetch it, or mark the account "needs refresh").
    • Long-term: contract tests (JSON fixtures per backend shard); schema validation in CI; consumer-driven contract with the backend team.
  7. Prevention: Golden-file tests for request bodies and responses; shadow-mode decode of responses with both parsers in a beta cohort; staged rollout with a crash and API-error alert tied to the migration flag; a "serialization behaviors" doc listing the Json config choices.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I'd not make every field nullable (hides contract violations and spreads null handling). I'd not set isLenient = true as a fix; it loosens parsing of malformed JSON, which is a different problem. I'd not re-add Gson alongside permanently.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Backend sends a new enum value your enum doesn't know. → Decoding fails; use coerceInputValues = true with a default or an UNKNOWN entry with a custom serializer.
  • Backend sends "balanceMinor": "1200" (string) sometimes. → Numbers as strings need a custom serializer or isLenient; prefer fixing the contract, add a serializer if you can't.
  • Does @SerialName matter with R8? → Not for correctness (no reflection), but it decouples wire names from Kotlin names for refactors.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Shadow decoding, where both parsers ran on a 5% cohort and a mismatch metric was logged, flagged 14 schema discrepancies a week before full rollout; the production incident rate after cutover was zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: makes all fields nullable, blames CDN.
  • Hire: explains encodeDefaults and missing-field strictness, proposes correct config and rollback.
  • Strong hire: separates the red herring, uses shadow decoding/fixtures/contract tests, and models backend reality in DTO vs domain layers.
